claim: Sleep slow oscillations and sleep spindles are associated with consolidation of Hebbian-based processes.
source: Sleep and plasticity are highly interrelated, as sleep slow oscillations and sleep spindles are associated with consolidation of Hebbian-based processes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: In adult humans, visual cortical plasticity is mainly sustained by homeostatic mechanisms.
source: However, in adult humans, visual cortical plasticity is mainly sustained by homeostatic mechanisms, for which the role of sleep is still largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Non-REM sleep stabilizes homeostatic plasticity of ocular dominance induced in adult humans by short-term monocular deprivation.
source: Here, we demonstrate that non-REM sleep stabilizes homeostatic plasticity of ocular dominance induced in adult humans by short-term monocular deprivation: the counterintuitive and otherwise transient boost of the deprived eye was preserved at the morning awakening (>6 hr after deprivation).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The boost of the deprived eye was preserved at the morning awakening (>6 hr after deprivation).
source: the counterintuitive and otherwise transient boost of the deprived eye was preserved at the morning awakening (>6 hr after deprivation).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Subjects exhibiting a stronger boost of the deprived eye after sleep had increased sleep spindle density in frontopolar electrodes.
source: Subjects exhibiting a stronger boost of the deprived eye after sleep had increased sleep spindle density in frontopolar electrodes, suggesting the involvement of distributed processes.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The individual susceptibility to visual homeostatic plasticity soon after deprivation correlated with the changes in sleep slow oscillations and spindle power in occipital sites.
source: Crucially, the individual susceptibility to visual homeostatic plasticity soon after deprivation correlated with the changes in sleep slow oscillations and spindle power in occipital sites, consistent with a modulation in early occipital visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: During non-REM sleep, replay, and pruning processes as well as connectivity rearrangements associated with specific neuronal activity patterns involving GABAergic modulation play a fundamental role in plasticity consolidation.
source: During non-REM (NREM) sleep, replay, and pruning processes as well as connectivity rearrangements associated with specific neuronal activity patterns involving GABAergic modulation (Ma et al., 2018) play a fundamental role in plasticity consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2018.

claim: SSOs and sleep spindles have been consistently associated with synaptic plasticity, replay, and memory consolidation.
source: SSOs and sleep spindles have been consistently associated with synaptic plasticity, replay, and memory consolidation (Rasch and Born, 2013; Crunelli et al., 2018; Antony et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The adult human visual system might retain a higher degree of plasticity than previously thought.
source: Growing evidence indicates that the adult human visual system might retain a higher degree of plasticity than previously thought (Castaldi et al., 2020; Baroncelli and Lunghi, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Some degree of Hebbian plasticity is retained in adulthood and mediates visual perceptual learning.
source: Some degree of Hebbian plasticity is retained in adulthood and mediates visual perceptual learning (Watanabe and Sasaki, 2015) as well as visuo-motor learning (Huber et al., 2004; Menicucci et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hebbian plasticity of ocular-dominance in the primary visual cortex (V1) is very weak or absent in primates after closure of visual critical period.
source: While sleep-dependent Hebbian plasticity has been shown in thalamocortical circuits in rodents visual system following prolonged exposure to a novel visual stimulus (Durkin et al., 2017), Hebbian plasticity of ocular-dominance in the primary visual cortex (V1) is very weak or absent in primates after closure of visual critical period.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation for the rodent case.

claim: In adult humans, short-term MD (2–2.5 hr) unexpectedly shifts ocular dominance in favour of the deprived eye.
source: in adult humans, recent studies have shown that short-term MD (2–2.5 hr) unexpectedly shifts ocular dominance in favour of the deprived eye (Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The deprived eye boost is observed also at the neural level, as revealed by EEG, MEG, and fMRI.
source: The deprived eye boost is observed also at the neural level, as revealed by EEG (Lunghi et al., 2015a), MEG (Chadnova et al., 2017), and fMRI (Binda et al., 2018; Kurzawski et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple neuroimaging studies.

claim: The deprived eye boost is mediated by a decrease of GABAergic inhibition in the V1.
source: and, importantly, it is mediated by a decrease of GABAergic inhibition in the V1 (Lunghi et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lunghi et al., 2015b.

claim: The effect of short-term MD decays within 90 min from eye-patch removal.
source: The effect of short-term MD decays within 90 min from eye-patch removal (Lunghi et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Repeated short-term deprivation of the amblyopic eye can promote the long-term recovery of both visual acuity and stereopsis in adult patients with anisometropic amblyopia.
source: However, recent evidence from a clinical study in adult patients with anisometropic amblyopia shows that repeated short-term deprivation of the amblyopic eye can promote the long-term recovery of both visual acuity and stereopsis (Lunghi et al., 2019b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: NREM sleep is necessary to consolidate Hebbian mechanisms during ocular dominance plasticity within the critical period in animal models.
source: Evidence from animal models shows that NREM sleep is necessary to consolidate Hebbian mechanisms during ocular dominance plasticity within the critical period (Aton et al., 2009; Durkin and Aton, 2019; Aton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Short-term MD shifted ocular dominance in favour of the deprived eye (mean DI ± SE = 0.77±0.04, t(18) = –5.41, p_fdr = 0.00017, Cohen's d=1.24).
source: Consistently with previous reports (Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2013), short-term MD shifted ocular dominance in favour of the deprived eye (Figure 1C, red symbols, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(4,72)=6.7, p<0.001, η2=0.27): the deprivation index (DI) was significantly altered just after eye-patch removal (mean DI ± SE = 0.77±0.04, two-tailed, one sample t-test t(18) = –5.41, p_fdr = 0.00017, Cohen's d=1.24).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity was maintained after 2 hr of sleep (mean DI ± SE = 0.87±0.04, t(18)=–3.54, p_fdr = 0.0046, Cohen's d=0.81).
source: Importantly, this form of homeostatic plasticity was maintained after 2 hr of sleep (mean DI ± SE = 0.87±0.04, two-tailed, one sample t-test t(18)=–3.54, p_fdr = 0.0046, Cohen's d=0.81)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity was maintained during the first 8 min after morning awakening (mean DI ± SE = 0.91±0.04, t(18)=–2.55, p_fdr = 0.02, Cohen's d=0.59), about 6–7 hr after eye-patch removal.
source: and during the first 8 min after morning awakening (mean DI ± SE = 0.91±0.04, two-tailed, one sample t-test t(18)=–2.55, p_fdr = 0.02, Cohen's d=0.59), that is about 6–7 hr after eye-patch removal.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No consistent changes in ocular dominance were observed in the control night (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(4,68)=0.97, p=0.43, η2=0.05).
source: No consistent changes in ocular dominance were observed in the control night (Figure 1C, black symbols, repeated-measures ANOVA, F(4,68)=0.97, p=0.43, η2=0.05), when calculating the same index for measurement at the same time but without MD.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of control condition data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The effect of MD (DI) measured before and after 2 hr of sleep did not correlate across subjects (Spearman's rho = 0.18, p=0.47).
source: Interestingly, the effect of MD (DI) measured before and after 2 hr of sleep did not correlate across subjects (Spearman's rho = 0.18, p=0.47).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The effect of MD decayed to baseline within 2 hr of darkness (mean DI ± SE = 1.03±0.07, t(16) = –0.04, p=0.96, Cohen's d=0.009).
source: In this experiment (Figure 2B, blue symbols), we found that the effect of MD (mean DI ± SE = 0.71±0.05, two-tailed, one-sample t-test, t(16)=–4.91, p<0.0002, Cohen's d=1.19) decayed to baseline within 2 hr of darkness (mean DI ± SE = 1.03±0.07, two-tailed, one-sample t-test, t(16) = –0.04, p=0.96, Cohen's d=0.009)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the dark exposure control experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a significant interaction between CONDITION and TIME for the decay of the effect of deprivation (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,16) = 4.48, p=0.05, η2=0.22), confirming the specific role of sleep in stabilizing visual homeostatic plasticity induced by MD.
source: We then directly compared the decay of the effect of deprivation after 2 hr of sleep (Figure 2B, red symbols) or after 2 hr of dark exposure (Figure 2B, blue symbols) by performing a 2 (TIME, before and after) × 2 (CONDITION, MDnight and MDmorn) repeated-measures ANOVA. We found a significant interaction between the factors CONDITION and TIME (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,16) = 4.48, p=0.05, η2=0.22), confirming the specific role of sleep in stabilizing visual homeostatic plasticity induced by MD.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison between sleep and dark exposure conditions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The MD effect was significantly larger when deprivation was performed in the morning (repeated-measures ANOVA, CONDITION: F(1,8)=6.87, p=0.031, η2=0.46), indicating a lower plastic potential of the visual cortex in the evening.
source: Moreover, the MD effect was significantly larger when deprivation was performed in the morning (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, repeated-measures ANOVA, CONDITION: F(1,8)=6.87, p=0.031, η2=0.46), indicating a lower plastic potential of the visual cortex in the evening.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the circadian control experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The changes from control to MD night of the rate of SSOs was correlated with the deprivation index measured before sleep (rho = −0.66, p=0.009, pfdr = 0.036).
source: For the SSOs, a strong correlation with plasticity was observed between changes in SSO rate (rho = −0.66, p=0.009, pfdr = 0.036, Figure 3, A)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The changes from control to MD night of the steepness of slope+ of SSOs was correlated with the deprivation index measured before sleep (rho = −0.64, p=0.012, pfdr = 0.037).
source: and shape (slope+, rho = −0.64, p=0.012, pfdr = 0.037, Figure 3, B
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The changes from control to MD night of the spindle power was correlated with the deprivation index measured before sleep (rho = −0.66, p=0.009, pfdr = 0.036).
source: Finally, for the sleep spindles, a correlation with plasticity was observed between their mean power (rho = −0.66, p=0.009, pfdr = 0.036; Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sleep spindles density in the prefrontal ROI strongly correlated with the effect of MD as maintained after sleep (rho = −0.74, p=0.002, pfdr = 0.04).
source: Sleep spindles density in the prefrontal ROI strongly correlated (rho = −0.74, p=0.002, pfdr = 0.04) with the effect of MD as maintained after sleep (Figure 4)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Participants retaining the stronger effect after 2 hr of sleep showed substantial increase of spindle density.
source: participants retaining the stronger effect after 2 hr of sleep showed substantial increase of spindle density.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sleep promotes the stabilization of visual homeostatic plasticity induced by 2 hr of MD.
source: We found that sleep promotes the stabilization of visual homeostatic plasticity induced by 2 hr of MD: the deprived eye boost observed after MD, which normally decays within 90 min of wakefulness (Lunghi et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013; Lunghi et al., 2011), is maintained by sleep for up to 6 hr after eye-patch removal.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data comparing sleep and dark exposure conditions.

claim: 2 hr of dark exposure after MD did not prevent the decay of the effect.
source: Importantly, this effect was specifically induced by sleep: 2 hr of dark exposure after MD did not prevent the decay of the effect.
evidence: This is supported by the dark exposure control experiment shown in Figure 2.

claim: The circadian rhythm did not influence the dynamics of the effect, as a similar time course of plasticity was observed when MD was performed early in the morning or late at night.
source: Finally, we found that the circadian rhythm did not influence the dynamics of the effect, as a similar time course of plasticity was observed when MD was performed early in the morning or late at night.
evidence: This is supported by the circadian control experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of SSO in visual areas reflects the interindividual variability in visual homeostatic plasticity.
source: We found that the expression of SSO in visual areas reflects the interindividual variability in visual homeostatic plasticity: their rate increased and their shape changed in occipital sites proportionally to the shift in ocular dominance induced by MD, as measured immediately before sleep.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Subjects with high visual plasticity show greater SSOs with steeper downstate exit slope (slope+) compared to their basal characteristics.
source: SSO shape changed accordingly after MD: subjects with high visual plasticity show greater SSOs with steeper downstate exit slope (slope+) compared to their basal characteristics.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression of oscillating activity in the sigma band changed as a function of the individual plastic potential of the visual cortex.
source: The expression of oscillating activity in the sigma band also changed as a function of the individual plastic potential of the visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: SSOs and sigma activity reflect the degree of homeostatic plasticity induced by short-term MD.
source: Overall, these results suggest that SSOs and sigma activity reflect the degree of homeostatic plasticity induced by short-term MD.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: GABA concentration measured after 2 hr of MD in V1 decreased proportionally to the observed ocular dominance shift.
source: Importantly, in humans, GABA concentration measured after 2 hr of MD in V1 decreased proportionally to the observed ocular dominance shift (Lunghi et al., 2015b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SWA expression increases in response to GABA agonists administration.
source: and SWA expression increases in response to GABA agonists administration (Faulhaber et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Complementary changes in the excitation/inhibition balance measured in the visual cortex of adult humans during NREM and REM sleep are correlated with visual plasticity induced by perceptual learning.
source: Interestingly, a recent study (Tamaki et al., 2020) reported that complementary changes in the excitation/inhibition balance measured in the visual cortex of adult humans during NREM and REM sleep are correlated with visual plasticity induced by perceptual learning
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Sleep oscillatory activity can reflect the plastic potential of the occipital cortex.
source: Sleep oscillatory activity can reflect the plastic potential of the occipital cortex: people highly susceptible to a visual manipulation (short-term MD) affecting V1 activity show increased SSO and sigma activity in occipital sites.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sleep can extend for many hours an otherwise transient unbalance of visual cortical activity.
source: Sleep can also extend for many hours an otherwise transient unbalance of visual cortical activity, and sleep spindles in prefrontal regions appear to support the process as subjects exhibiting stronger maintenance had increased frontopolar sleep spindle density, as it occurs for many memory consolidation processes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings shown in Figures 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Nineteen healthy volunteers (mean age ± SD 24.8±3.7 years, range 21–33 years; 8 males) participated in the main study.
source: Nineteen healthy volunteers (mean age ± SD 24.8±3.7 years, range 21–33 years; 8 males), participated in the main study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity (ETDRS charts).
source: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity (ETDRS charts).
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: MD was performed by applying a custom-made eye-patch on the dominant eye.
source: MD was performed by applying a custom-made eye-patch on the dominant eye.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The eye-patch was made of a translucent plastic material that allows light to reach the retina (attenuation 15%) but completely prevents pattern vision.
source: The eye-patch was made of a translucent plastic material that allows light to reach the retina (attenuation 15%) but completely prevents pattern vision.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: MD lasted 2 hr.
source: MD lasted 2 hr, during which participants stayed in the laboratory control room under experimenters' supervision and did activities such as reading and working on the computer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: EEG was recorded using a Net Amps 300 system with a 128-electrodes HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net.
source: EEG was recorded using a Net Amps 300 system (Electrical Geodesic Inc, Eugene, OR) with a 128-electrodes HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment.

claim: Participants fell asleep easily and fast (sleep latency 9±2 min – mean ± SE).
source: According to EEG recordings, in the night sessions participants fell asleep easily and fast (sleep latency 9±2 min – mean ± SE)
evidence: This is a description of the sleep characteristics of participants.

claim: Participants showed a normal organization of sleep structure (37±3% spent in N2 stage, and 50±3% spent in N3 stage, on average).
source: showed a normal organization of sleep structure (37±3% spent in N2 stage, and 50±3% spent in N3 stage, on average)
evidence: This is a description of the sleep characteristics of participants.

claim: Participants exhibited none or few minutes of REM sleep (9±2 min).
source: exhibited none (8 out of 15 subjects in the MDnight and 4 out of 15 subjects in the Cnight) or few minutes of REM sleep (9±2 min)
evidence: This is a description of the sleep characteristics of participants.

claim: None of the participants had wakefulness episodes after sleep onset.
source: and none of them had wakefulness episodes after sleep onset.
evidence: This is a description of the sleep characteristics of participants.

claim: The alteration of SSO shape and density observed at the occipital level during the sleep immediately following MD might reflect the change in GABA concentration induced by deprivation.
source: We speculate that the alteration of SSO shape and density observed at the occipital level during the sleep immediately following MD might reflect the change in GABA concentration induced by deprivation and be a neurophysiological marker of the interindividual variability in the level of plasticity in adult humans.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: The alteration of SSO shape and density might be a neurophysiological marker of the interindividual variability in the level of plasticity in adult humans.
source: We speculate that the alteration of SSO shape and density observed at the occipital level during the sleep immediately following MD might reflect the change in GABA concentration induced by deprivation and be a neurophysiological marker of the interindividual variability in the level of plasticity in adult humans.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: Individual sleep pattern could interact with visual homeostatic plasticity.
source: This suggests that individual sleep pattern could interact with visual homeostatic plasticity and that the instatement and maintenance of plasticity might be mediated by different neural processes, possibly reflected in different features of NREM sleep.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between DI before and after sleep.

claim: The instatement and maintenance of plasticity might be mediated by different neural processes, possibly reflected in different features of NREM sleep.
source: This suggests that individual sleep pattern could interact with visual homeostatic plasticity and that the instatement and maintenance of plasticity might be mediated by different neural processes, possibly reflected in different features of NREM sleep.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between DI before and after sleep.

claim: The effect of MD may be overall underestimated.
source: This might reflect a transient form of adaptation or implicit learning due to the repetition of the BR test (Klink et al., 2010), suggesting that the effect of MD may be overall underestimated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of a small effect in the control night.

claim: Sleep maintained visual homeostatic plasticity, stabilizing the ocular dominance change induced by MD and delaying the expected decay until the awakening.
source: Our results therefore indicate that sleep maintained visual homeostatic plasticity, stabilizing the ocular dominance change induced by MD and delaying the expected decay until the awakening.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The maintenance of the MD effect is specific to sleep.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the maintenance of the MD effect is specific to sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing sleep and dark exposure conditions.

claim: The lower plastic potential observed in the evening indicates that the role of NREM sleep in stabilizing homeostatic ocular dominance plasticity might be underestimated.
source: Moreover, the lower plastic potential observed in the evening indicates that the role of NREM sleep in stabilizing homeostatic ocular dominance plasticity might be underestimated.
evidence: This is inferred from the circadian control experiment results.

claim: No sleep architecture parameters varied significantly between nights or were associated with DI measurements.
source: No sleep architecture parameters varied significantly between nights or were associated with DI measurements.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis of sleep architecture parameters.

claim: We never observed any main changes of the sleep rhythms or features between MDnight and Cnight recordings, in any of the ROIs.
source: We never observed any main changes of the sleep rhythms or features between MDnight and Cnight recordings, in any of the ROIs (Table in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis comparing sleep features between conditions.

claim: Subjects showing a stronger plasticity effect showed increased SSO rate.
source: subjects showing a stronger plasticity effect showed (1) increased SSO rate
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Subjects showing a stronger plasticity effect showed increased sharpness of transitions from the SSO negative peak.
source: (2) increased sharpness of transitions from the SSO negative peak
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Subjects with lower plasticity effect exhibited opposite parameters changes.
source: whereas subjects with lower plasticity effect exhibited opposite parameters changes.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: The opposite changes between subjects with high and low plasticity, without any main effect of MD manipulation on SSO features, suggest different local synchronization in the sleeping neurons undergoing the bistability behaviour of SSO.
source: The opposite changes between subjects with high and low plasticity, without any main effect of MD manipulation on SSO features, suggest different local synchronization in the sleeping neurons undergoing the bistability behaviour of SSO.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: Power of sleep spindles over the occipital sites increased in the MDnight for participants showing higher visual homeostatic plasticity.
source: power of sleep spindles over the occipital sites increased in the MDnight for participants showing higher visual homeostatic plasticity (i.e. a large boost of the deprived eye)
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The power of sleep spindles was reduced in participants showing a lower response to MD.
source: while the power was reduced in participants showing a lower response to MD.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sigma activity power expressed during the whole NREM sleep in the occipital ROI correlated with individual ocular dominance shifts (rho = −0.66, p=0.009, pfdr = 0.036).
source: Indeed, sigma activity power expressed during the whole NREM sleep in the occipital ROI correlated with individual ocular dominance shifts (rho = −0.66, p=0.009, pfdr = 0.036, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, B)
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, B.

claim: The sigma rhythm expressed just before SSO events correlated with individual ocular dominance shifts (rho = −0.70, p=0.0046, pfdr = 0.025).
source: and overlapping result was observed when considering the sigma rhythm expressed just before SSO events that favour the emergence of full-fledged SSO (rho = −0.70, p=0.0046, pfdr = 0.025, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, C).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, C.

claim: No correlation was observed between the power of SWA during the whole NREM sleep with the plasticity index.
source: These strong correlations contrast with the absence of association with the power of SWA during the whole NREM sleep with the plasticity index (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, D.

claim: The observed significant correlations were coherent at the single electrode level within the occipital ROI.
source: The observed significant correlations were coherent at the single electrode level within the occipital ROI (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by the single electrode analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlations were not observed in the sensory-motor ROI or at the electrode level within this control ROI.
source: but they were not observed in the sensory-motor ROI or at the electrode level within this control ROI.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the ROI analysis.

claim: No correlation between EEG rhythms power and visual plasticity was observed in the control experiment (darkness exposure condition).
source: Also they were specific for sleep as no correlation between EEG rhythms power and visual plasticity was observed in the control experiment (darkness exposure condition, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the control experiment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: No correlation was observed between spindle density and DI after sleep in the occipital and sensory-motor ROIs.
source: No correlation was observed in the other ROIs.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the correlation analysis for spindle density.

claim: Neither power of SWA and sigma bands, nor SSO rate and shape, were associated with the residual eye dominance after 2 hr of sleep.
source: Besides, neither power of SWA and sigma bands, nor SSO rate and shape, were associated with the residual eye dominance after 2 hr of sleep (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the EEG measures was associated with the residual eye dominance after 2 hr of sleep (DI after).
source: Among the considered EEG measures (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), none was associated with the residual eye dominance after 2 hr of sleep (DI after).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis of EEG parameter variations during sleep shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: NREM sleep has an effect on ocular dominance plasticity also past the critical period in humans.
source: Here, we show for the first time that NREM sleep has an effect on ocular dominance plasticity also past the critical period in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The homeostatic plasticity process triggered by MD is associated with up-regulation of the deprived eye activity.
source: The homeostatic plasticity process triggered by MD is associated with up-regulation of the deprived eye activity, but also with down-regulation of the non-deprived eye at the level of the V1 (Lunghi et al., 2015a; Chadnova et al., 2017; Binda et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NREM sleep appears to intervene in a rebalancing process involving overall visual cortical activity.
source: NREM sleep appears therefore to intervene in a rebalancing process involving overall visual cortical activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results showing opposite changes for deprived and non-deprived eyes.

claim: This rebalancing process operates in opposite directions for the deprived and non-deprived eye.
source: This rebalancing process operates in opposite directions for the deprived and non-deprived eye
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on MD effects.

claim: The rebalancing process explains the lack of an association between sleep features at the occipital level and the maintenance of the MD effect observed after sleep.
source: which explains the lack of an association between sleep features at the occipital level and the maintenance of the MD effect observed after sleep
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of correlation between occipital sleep features and DI after sleep.

claim: The rebalancing process explains the lack of a main effect of MD on the subsequent sleep features.
source: as well as the lack of a main effect of MD on the subsequent sleep features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of main effects of MD on sleep features.

claim: The influence of sleep on ocular dominance plasticity was reflected by some sleep features in high-level areas, indicating a role of extra-striate cortex in regulating visual plasticity in adults.
source: Interestingly, we found that the influence of sleep on ocular dominance plasticity was reflected by some sleep features in high-level areas, indicating a role of extra-striate cortex in regulating visual plasticity in adults.
evidence: This is inferred from the prefrontal spindle density correlation with DI after sleep.

claim: The consolidation of several forms of plasticity has been associated with sleep spindle density.
source: indeed the consolidation of several forms of plasticity has been associated with sleep spindle density (Clemens et al., 2005; Gais et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some forms of visual plasticity (e.g. perceptual learning) are reflected in changed activity and connectivity within the hippocampus.
source: and some forms of visual plasticity (e.g. perceptual learning) are reflected in changed activity and connectivity within the hippocampus (Urner et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The hippocampus has dense anatomical connections with the V1.
source: which has dense anatomical connections with the V1 (Maller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The V1 may be under hippocampal control in wakefulness, as visual memory may require replay activity.
source: However, we cannot exclude that the V1 may be under hippocampal control in wakefulness, as visual memory may require replay activity.
evidence: This is stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: Simple orientation texture discrimination tasks are also stabilized during sleep and frontal activity are implicated in the stabilization process.
source: Interestingly, simple orientation texture discrimination tasks are also stabilized during sleep and also in these case frontal activity are implicated in the stabilization process (Yamada, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Activity in non-visual areas plays a role in modulating the decay of short-term visual plasticity in adult humans.
source: Altogether, consistent with other results, we show that activity in non-visual areas plays a role in modulating the decay of short-term visual plasticity in adult humans
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the prefrontal spindle density results.

claim: Activity in non-visual areas might be crucial to promote the stabilization of the plastic changes induced by MD that was observed in amblyopic patients.
